📌 Zcash sets July 28 hard fork to seal Orchard after critical bug 

⚠️ Zcash founder Zooko Wilcox has explained how the network’s July 28 Ironwood hard fork will address uncertainty around a critical flaw in the Orchard shielded pool. The upgrade will not identify or freeze individual counterfeit coins. Instead, it will seal the old pool and limit how much ZEC can leave. 

🔖 Ironwood, also known as NU6.3, is scheduled to activate at block 3,428,143 on July 28. The upgrade will retire the current Orchard pool and introduce a new shielded pool based on the corrected circuit. According to Zcash’s official Ironwood user update, users will no longer be able to send or receive ZEC inside the old Orchard pool after activation. Funds can leave only through the turnstile, which prevents more ZEC from exiting than legitimately entered.

⭐️ The Zcash team said it believes the flaw was “unlikely to have been exploited,” but users cannot independently prove no counterfeit ZEC was created. Ironwood aims to trap any excess value inside the old pool rather than allow it to enter wider circulation. Security researcher Taylor Hornby discovered the Orchard flaw on May 29 while auditing the shielded system. The bug could have allowed an attacker to create counterfeit ZEC inside Orchard without leaving an obvious public record.

The Real Gold Rush: Expanding the Surface

The Strategy of Blinding: Why Iran Is Keeping Israel Out of the Fight — For Now
By researcher A.

There is a fascinating paradox in the way Iran is managing the current escalation in the Middle East. While it is setting the region ablaze, it also appears to be making a deliberate effort to avoid drawing Israel directly into the conflict. This is likely neither accidental nor the result of deterrence, but rather a calculated strategic decision.

To understand Iran’s approach, one must understand the difference between the campaign being fought now and the one Iran is actually preparing for.

The Existential War vs. the Tactical Campaign

Iran’s current successes are based on applying pressure to Arab states and to the American military presence in the region. Its objective is to wear down its opponents, extract concessions, reshape the regional balance of deterrence, and force the West into compromises or withdrawals.

Israel, however, is a different story.

If Iran were to attack Israel directly, it would lose this indirect leverage and enter an entirely different arena. Israel does not fight limited engagements merely to reach a negotiated settlement. If Israel enters a full-scale war, it does so from the perspective of an existential conflict.

Israel has a structured, precise, and comprehensive war plan. It would not seek a symbolic victory leading to a ceasefire on Iranian terms, but would instead focus on systematically destroying military capabilities.

Iran understands this well. That is why, at least for now, Israel remains outside the equation.

The Trap for Israel

But this is precisely where the danger lies.

The fact that Iran currently seeks to avoid a direct confrontation with Israel does not mean it is not preparing the battlefield for the day when such a confrontation becomes unavoidable.

Iran’s actions throughout the Middle East reflect a familiar operational concept: to “blind” Israel by gradually stripping away its regional layers of defense, so that when the decisive moment arrives, Israel will stand increasingly isolated and be forced to rely almost exclusively on its own defensive systems.

This pattern is not new.

For years, studies—including research conducted by the Jerusalem Center for Security and Foreign Affairs (formerly JCPA) under the leadership of Brig. Gen. (Res.) Yossi Kuperwasser—have described Hezbollah’s doctrine of systematically targeting the “eyes” of the IDF: radars, surveillance systems, and intelligence collection assets, in order to degrade Israel’s ability to detect launches and gather real-time intelligence.

Iran is now applying the same concept—but on a regional scale.

First, it targets regional radar and early-warning systems through attacks on American bases.

Second, it seeks to weaken the American defensive umbrella. Recent footage suggests that American interceptor batteries have struggled—and in some cases failed—to cope with large missile barrages.

Third, it employs missiles with hypersonic characteristics, alongside cruise missiles and drones, with increasingly accurate strikes against defensive systems themselves.

Preparing Israel to Stand Alone

Iran may not want Israel to enter the war today, but it is certainly working to ensure that when the day comes, Israel will face it largely alone.

As the region’s defensive layers erode, Gulf radar systems are degraded, and American interception capabilities are weakened, the burden increasingly shifts to Israel’s own air-defense network—Arrow, David’s Sling, and Iron Dome.

These are outstanding systems, among the best in the world. Yet, as past experience has demonstrated, even they cannot provide absolute protection against massive barrages of fast, highly accurate missiles launched simultaneously from multiple fronts.

It is therefore essential not to mistake Iran’s current reluctance to confront Israel directly for genuine deterrence.

The relative quiet Israel currently enjoys on the direct front is not a gift. It is time that Iran is using to systematically erode the defensive shield surrounding Israel.

Trump: 50% Tariffs On Most Canadian Goods

🔠🔠🔠🔠1️⃣

Trump is imposing 50% tariffs on most Canadian goods in response to the country retaliating against previous US tariffs, the White House announced Monday, declaring Canada has unfairly discriminated against American cars, alcohol and dairy products.

The tariffs will hit a wide range of products, the White House said, including wine, hockey sticks and cement. They also include goods previously protected from import taxes under the United States-Mexico-Canada (USMCA) agreement.

The new tariffs will exclude energy products, fish, critical minerals and potash. They also exclude products already subject to tariffs aimed at protecting national security, such as steel and aluminum.

The steep tariffs will probably unleash a new wave of economic chaos, with risks of higher inflation and further fraying of relations between two nations that had been closely woven together before Trump’s return to the White House.

The Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, said in a statement that his government has made comprehensive proposals ‌to resolve trade disputes with Washington, asserting that Trump’s past tariffs violated ‌a trade pact between the two countries.

“This trade dispute has raised costs for families, particularly in the US,” he said. “Canada stands ready to engage intensively to address outstanding issues with the US to the mutual benefit of our citizens.”

The White House said the tariffs will go into effect in 30 days, leaving time for possible negotiations between the two countries.

Trump signed three proclamations to launch the tariffs under Section 338 of the 1930 Trade Act. Several Democratic lawmakers last year proposed repealing the section because they said Trump could use it to destabilize the economy.

A White House fact sheet claims Trump is “taking action to hold Canada accountable for its continued discrimination against and unreasonable and unequal treatment of U.S. commerce that has burdened and disadvantaged hardworking Americans”.

Trump claims in the proclamations that Canada discriminates against American automobiles, alcohol and cheese relative to other nations, but his argument rests in large part on retaliatory actions taken by Canada after the US president imposed tariffs on Canada under the pretext that it should do more to stop fentanyl smuggling into the US.

Trump noted in his autos proclamation that Canada maintained, starting in April 2025, a 25% tariff on the imports of US motor vehicles that did not qualify for preferential treatment under the USMCA.

The White House also cited all but two Canadian provinces and territories stopping the sale of US alcoholic beverages, while not imposing similar restrictions on other countries.

Trump also objected to Canada’s treatment of US cheese, saying in his proclamation that Canada discriminates against the US compared to Europe on dairy products.
